catalog_quote: Word stress falls on the final syllable of nouns and pronouns. ..neither the indefinite or the definite article (-i -ra) carries stress (these are affixed to the end of the noun stem).. (Lambton 1953:7)
sweep_summary: Persian (west2369, catalog fixed-strict final; deciding quote Lambton 1953:7 via StressTyp2, check CSV names Amini 1997). Of the 10 works with stress in the title, 5 were obtained and read in full: Hosseini 2014 (UTokyo dissertation, 209 pp., open repository) is the best new first-hand statement — final stress in nouns/adjectives/verb roots/most adverbs and in compounds and derivations, inflectional suffixes stressless except -hâ/-ân, -tar/-tarin, -e, verb prefixes prominent, Arabic-loan particles initially stressed — confirming the final coding and refining its edges; Modarresi 2014 (HU Berlin dissertation) is sentence-level prosody and silent on word stress; the two Taheri-Ardali Speech Prosody focus papers (2012, 2014) are silent on placement. A bonus open paper found on the same ISCA index, Abolhasanizadeh 2012 (SP 2012), states 'Final syllables of nouns, adjectives, most adverbs and unprefixed verbs have the stress. Prefixed verbs take stress on the prefix' and shows f0 alone cues the location. Paywalled and not read: Ferguson 1957 (abstract obtained: stress contrastive, máhi vs mahí; priority high), Kahnemuyipour 2003 NLLT (summarised by Hosseini; open 2000 precursor already. medium) and Abolhasanizadeh et al. 2012 Lingua (summarised by Hosseini and its SP companion; medium). Not found: Mahjani 2003 (Edinburgh MSc, intonation) and Eslami 2000 (Tehran PhD, Persian, sentence prosody), both low priority. Falahati 2020 is L2-acquisition, not relevant. everything came from repository APIs, ISCA archive, Crossref and automated download.

new_statements.quote: In nouns, adjectives, verb roots and most adverbs, the rightmost syllable is metrically strong (stressed). Every lexical word in Persian has one and only one stressed syllable and the place of stress does not depend on the weight or the number of syllables ... even in long words containing heavy syllables, only the rightmost syllable is stressed. ... Compound nouns and adjectives as well, have only one stress on the last syllable of the compound, regardless of the word length. ... Inflectional suffixes on the other hand, fall out of the stress domain and are always stressless.
new_statements.citation: Hosseini, Seyed Ayat (2014). The phonology and phonetics of prosodic prominence in Persian. Doctoral dissertation, University of Tokyo (repository record 6575, file; hdl 2261/57678; doi 10.15083/00006566).
new_statements.reading: Fixed final stress on the lexical word (nouns, adjectives, verb roots, most adverbs; compounds and derivations included), weight- and length-insensitive, with inflectional suffixes and clitics outside the domain — this confirms the catalog's final-syllable coding for nouns. The same pages refine it: the plural -hâ/-ân, comparative/superlative -tar/-tarin and perfective -e DO attract stress (pedar-hấ, bad-tár, mord-é), conjugated verbs are prominent on the leftmost prefix (mí-xând-am), and a closed set of (mostly Arabic-loan) discourse particles is initially stressed (§3.7, p. 60). Together with the earlier-held Rahmani/Gussenhoven line, Hosseini treats the prominence as a single edgemost 'stress' realised as a pitch accent. Nothing read contradicts 'final' as the dominant pattern; the counts as exceptionless (the strict set) register remains the point of caution (verb prefixes, particles).

new_statements.quote: A summary of stress points in Persian includes the following. For nouns, adjectives, and most adverbs, the stress is word-final. [...] Polymorphemic nouns, adjectives, and adverbs have the above pattern too, i.e., have final stress [...] Verbs have their stress on the final syllable of the main constituent, i.e., the present stem, the past stem, or the participle. [...] However, the negative marker ne-/næ-, the durative prefix mi-, and the subjunctive/imperative prefix be- attract the stress [...] Enclitics and certain suffixes such as the indefinite marker –i (as in ketáb-i "a book") do not affect stress. There are a few morphologically simple words, mostly of Arabic origin, which are stressed word-initially.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final syllable) and the Hosseini 2014 statement; adds the verb-prefix stress hierarchy (ne- > mi- > be-), the future-auxiliary exception, compound-verb stress on the non-verbal element, the closed initially-stressed particle set, and the vocative initial-stress pattern with a 5-speaker judgement test. Also notes that pitch accents sit on the lexically stressed syllable (citing Eslami & Bijankhan 2002).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical stress falls on the final syllable of nouns, adjectives and most adverbs, including polymorphemic and compound ones (plural -ha, derivational -i, comparative -tær, prefix ba- all take final stress: šune-há, šad-í, ab-limú, kutah-tǽr, ba-sævád, movæqqæt-ǽn). Verbs are stressed on the final syllable of the stem/participle (xær-íd-æm), but the negative ne-/næ-, durative mi- and subjunctive/imperative be- prefixes attract stress (né-mi-xær-id-æm), ne-/næ- outranking mi-. Enclitics and the indefinite -i are outside the stress domain. Pitch accents (L+H* on finally stressed words, H* on initially stressed words and monosyllables) dock on the lexically stressed syllable. Variety: Modern Conversational Persian of Tehran.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Persian (secondary stress is mentioned only for English on p. 8xx of the chapter 7 comparison).
new_statements.exceptions: Future tense stressed on the final syllable of the auxiliary (xah-ǽm-ræft, p. 24); compound verbs and prefixal verbs stressed on the non-verbal element (geryé+kærd, vá+ræft), a lexicalised subset stressed like simple verbs (bær+gǽšt-æn, p. 25); a few morphologically simple mostly Arabic-origin words are initially stressed (ǽmma 'but', bǽle 'yes', p. 25); vocatives are stressed on the initial syllable in all words and phrases (§7.1, p. 163: 'the consultants unanimously judged the stress for citation forms on the ultimate syllable and for vocatives on the initial syllable').
new_statements.identity_note: Sadat-Tehrani states (§1.3, p. 20-21) that the dialect under study is Modern Conversational Persian as spoken in Tehran, recorded from 8 native speakers; the stress summary is for that variety, which is the standard Iranian Persian the catalog codes.

[p. 36:] Ausnahmen: erstsilbenbetont (baryton) sind: einzelne arab. LW: ámmā „aber“, válī ... yáʿnī „das heißt“, bále „ja“ u.a.; einige persische Konjunktionen bzw. new_statements.translation: 2.3.1. Rule: All words of New Persian are stressed on the last syllable (oxytone); suffix syllables count just like stem syllables: pedár 'father' – pedarā́n 'fathers' – pedarāné 'fatherly', xāné 'house' – xānehā́ 'houses', bozórg 'big' – bozorghā́ 'big (pl.)' ... Enclitics, unlike suffixes, are not stressed: xāné-rā 'the house (obj.)', xāné-ī 'a house', xāné-ye bozórg 'the big house' ... pedár-am 'my father' ... There are exceptions in the verbal system. The personal endings of the preterite are unstressed; the prefixes mī- and na- and all preverbs are dominantly stressed. [p. 36:] Exceptions: initially stressed (barytone) are: individual Arabic loanwords: ámmā 'but', válī ..., yáʿnī 'that is', bále 'yes' etc.; some Persian conjunctions or particles ...: mágar, hár čand (ke), mábādā, ágarče etc. (cf. Lambton 74).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is word-final: on the last syllable of the noun/adjective stem, moving to the last syllable of any plural, comparative/superlative or derivational suffix (ketâb, ketâb-hấ, ketâb-che-hấ; kuchek-tár, kuchek-tarín, kuchek-í). In verbs (p. 21) the prefixes mi-, be- and na- attract stress; otherwise stress is on the last syllable of the stem or participle; agreement suffixes never affect stress (except in the formal future, where the auxiliary's agreement syllable bears main stress, fn. 17). Unstressed 'particles' after Lazard: -o 'and', ke, ham, vocative -â, indefinite -i, relative -i, -râ, Ezafe -e, the copula, pronominal enclitics (§1.3.2, pp. 21-22). The author uses stress-attraction as the diagnostic separating derivational (stress-affecting) from inflectional (non-stress-affecting) affixes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In compound nouns main stress on the final syllable of the second member, secondary stress on the final syllable of the first member; the secondary stress disappears in very common compounds (p. 18, ex. 13 fârsi zabân, tâze vâred).
new_statements.exceptions: Discourse-initial words / words in isolation (after Lazard 1992: 38-9); verbal prefixes mi-, be-, na- attract stress; agreement suffixes, enclitics, indefinite/relative -i, -râ, Ezafe -e, -o, ke, ham, vocative -â unstressed; formal future stresses the auxiliary's agreement morpheme (fn. 17); numeral+classifier indefinite reading stresses the numeral (dó nafar, p. later ch.).

tone_statements.quote: Although Persian word prominence has been described as “word stress” ..., recent experimental evidence shows that it is realized only through fundamental frequency (F0) (Abolhasanizadeh et al. 2012). Thus, in technical terms, it is an accent, a tone in a specific location, like the lexical (prosodic) prominence in Japanese ... Phonologically, the Persian accent consists of a H tone. ... Persian has a small tonal inventory. In addition to the accent (H), there are two intonational boundary tones: L% for declaratives and Wh-questions, and (L)H% for yes/no questions.
tone_statements.summary: Word prominence analysed as a tonal accent: one H tone on the final syllable of each morphological word, cued by F0 alone, deleted after focus and in factive clauses; clitics unaccented.

tone_statements.citation: Abolhasani Zadeh, Vahideh, Carlos Gussenhoven & Mahmood Bijankhan. 2010. The position of clitics in Persian intonational structure. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2010 (Chicago), paper 108. doi:10.21437/speechprosody.2010-60.
tone_statements.quote: Most importantly, a pitch accent (L+)H* is associated with the word-final (i.e. base-final) syllable of clitic groups, but with the word-final syllable of words, meaning that clitics remain outside the domain of the word. The pitch accent marks the stress, but we found no independent durational or spectral differences between stressed and unstressed syllables. ... Unlike Germanic, Persian post-focal words are accented, though pronounced with reduced pitch range.

tone_statements.summary: One pitch accent (L+)H* on the word-final syllable, clitics skipped; no stress cues independent of the accent; post-focal accents kept in reduced pitch range.

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict, final syllable' rests on Amini 1997 (TWPL phonology paper), whose three deciding passages are verbatim in the held scanned at the stated pages (1, 2, 4). Two held dissertations (Sadat-Tehrani 2007 p. 22; Rohany Rahbar 2012) and four open sources downloaded now (Kahnemuyipour 2000 ZASPiL pp. 120/122; Rahmani et al. 2015 PLoS ONE p. 4; Rahmani et al. 2016; Rahmani 2018) all state that nouns/adjectives, simple, derived or compound, carry prominence on the final syllable, clitics excluded; prefixed verbs take prefix stress. No source contradicts the position. The refinement worth a caution note, not a reclassify: Rahmani, Rietveld & Gussenhoven (2015-2018) argue the final prominence is a post-lexical f0 accent (Persian listeners are stress-'deaf'), i.e. the language may lack lexical stress proper while the surface rule stays right-edge.
